## Most likely cause

Two findings in the same causal chain explain a date-boundary flake better than anything else in this scan:

**1. `generateInvoice` reads the wall clock 7 separate times** — `crime_00018`, `src/billing.ts` lines 57, 63, 92, 198, 238, 250, 273 (5× `Date.now()`, 2× `new Date()`), spread across a 204-line body (`crime_00004`, lines 50–253).

Nothing pins those reads to a single instant. Every call re-observes the clock, so if execution straddles a boundary — midnight, month end, billing-period rollover — line 57 and line 250 disagree about what day it is. That's precisely the shape of a test that passes 99 runs and fails the 100th: the failure window is milliseconds wide and only opens near a boundary.

**2. The date helpers mix time domains** — `crime_00003`, `src/date.ts`: receiver `d` uses `getUTCFullYear()` @L9 and `getMonth()` @L41.

The two method families differ silently by the host's UTC offset. Any date within the offset distance of midnight lands in a *different day, month, or year* depending on which family reads it. Combined with `crime_00008` (`"2026-12-25T07:00:00"` @L29 and `"2026-12-20"` @L33 parsed with no timezone marker — the bare-date form parses as UTC, the datetime form as local), the same nominal date enters the system in two different domains.

**Diagnosis:** finding 2 is *why it's wrong at boundaries*; finding 1 is *why it's intermittent instead of constant*. If the failure also correlates with CI vs. laptop rather than with time-of-day, finding 2 alone is sufficient — CI runs in UTC, so the local-family reads shift by your local offset.

**Why nobody caught it:** `crime_00019` and `crime_00037` — `src/billing.test.ts` has one test with **zero assertions** ("renders the enterprise plan", L4–6) and one with a single weak matcher ("creates an invoice", L8–10). There is currently no test protecting date behaviour at all.

## Secondary suspect

`crime_00010` — `src/date.ts:52` adds `86400000` to advance a day. That is correct 363 days a year and wrong on the two DST transition days, where a calendar day is 23 or 25 hours. If the failing case is a specific date rather than a specific time, check this first.

## Proposed fix

**Step 1 — pin the clock (fixes the flakiness).** Capture the instant once at the boundary and thread it through:

```ts
export function generateInvoice(input: InvoiceInput, asOf: Date = new Date()) {
  // every downstream period/due-date calculation takes `asOf`,
  // no further Date.now() below this line
}
```

This collapses 7 independent clock reads into one, and lets a test pass `new Date("2026-01-31T23:59:59.500Z")` deterministically.

**Step 2 — pick one time domain (fixes the wrongness).** Make all billing arithmetic UTC: convert `getMonth()` @L41 to `getUTCMonth()` so receiver `d` is uniformly UTC, and convert to local only in `toLocaleDateString()` at the display boundary (`crime_00025` @L46 — pass an explicit locale there too, e.g. `'en-US'`).

**Step 3 — make the literals explicit.** `"2026-12-20"` → `"2026-12-20T00:00:00Z"`, `"2026-12-25T07:00:00"` → `"2026-12-25T07:00:00Z"` (or a real `±HH:MM` offset if 07:00 was meant as a local wall-clock time).

**Step 4 — replace the ms arithmetic.** `+ 86400000` @L52 → a calendar-aware `addDays` (Temporal, Luxon, or `date-fns-tz`).

**Step 5 — lock it down.** Replace the two no-op tests with a table pinned via the injected `asOf`, covering: last-instant-of-month (`23:59:59.999`), first-instant-of-month, a leap-day, and a DST transition date — run under both `TZ=UTC` and `TZ=America/New_York`. Step 1 is what makes those tests possible at all.

Do steps 1–3 together as one change; they're the same bug seen from three angles, and fixing the clock without unifying the time domain will just make the wrong answer deterministic.

---

One note on the tool run itself: you scoped the scan to `src/billing.ts`, but the output covers all 19 files in the repo (SVG assets, nav registry, routes). That was useful here — the root cause lives in `src/date.ts`, not `billing.ts` — but the path argument doesn't appear to have filtered anything.
